series.name: Top 20 categories by 12-month sales
series.note: Baru Sahib retail only (all 12-month sales sit under LocationID 15). Hunger Heroes (002CM) excluded. Sales are the till value net of returns; 'per resident' divides by the stated campus population of 5,000. Out of stock = total on-hand across every warehouse at or below zero. The 'unsold 90+ days' column separates a real stockout from a fresh-produce artefact: Fruits shows 38 empty lines but only 11 have gone unsold for 90 days, because bananas are counted at zero every night. Confectionery and Personal Care carry no such excuse — 422 and 449 lines are both empty and dormant. FULL QUERY: WITH sku AS (SELECT pm.ProductGroupID AS gid, sd.ProductID AS pid, SUM(sd.FinalSaleAmount) AS amt, MAX(sh.VoucherDate) AS last_sale FROM SaleDetail sd JOIN SaleHeader sh ON sh.SerialNumber = sd.SerialNumber JOIN ProductMaster pm ON pm.ProductID = sd.ProductID WHERE sh.VoucherDate >= '2025-09-01' AND sh.VoucherDate < '2026-09-01' AND sh.CustomerID <> '002CM' GROUP BY pm.ProductGroupID, sd.ProductID), st AS (SELECT ProductID, SUM(Quantity) AS q FROM Stock GROUP BY ProductID), j AS (SELECT sku.*, ISNULL(st.q,0) AS q FROM sku LEFT JOIN st ON st.ProductID = sku.pid), ret AS (SELECT pm.ProductGroupID AS gid, SUM(rd.FinalSaleAmount) AS r FROM SaleReturnDetail rd JOIN SaleReturnHeader rh ON rh.SerialNumber = rd.SerialNumber JOIN ProductMaster pm ON pm.ProductID = rd.ProductID WHERE rh.VoucherDate >= '2025-09-01' AND rh.VoucherDate < '2026-09-01' AND rh.CustomerID <> '002CM' GROUP BY pm.ProductGroupID), act AS (SELECT ProductGroupID AS gid, COUNT(*) AS active FROM ProductMaster WHERE IsActive = 1 GROUP BY ProductGroupID), g AS (SELECT gid, COUNT(*) AS sold_skus, SUM(amt) AS gross, SUM(CASE WHEN q <= 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS oos, SUM(CASE WHEN q <= 0 THEN amt ELSE 0 END) AS gross_oos, SUM(CASE WHEN q <= 0 AND DATEDIFF(day,last_sale,'2026-08-30') > 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS gone90 FROM j GROUP BY gid) SELECT TOP 20 pg.ProductGroupName AS category, ISNULL(act.active,0) AS active_skus, g.sold_skus, g.oos, CAST(100.0*g.oos/g.sold_skus AS DECIMAL(6,1)) AS oos_pct, g.gone90, CAST(g.gross - ISNULL(ret.r,0) AS DECIMAL(18,2)) AS net_sales_12m, CAST((g.gross - ISNULL(ret.r,0))/5000.0 AS DECIMAL(12,0)) AS per_resident_yr, CAST(g.gross_oos AS DECIMAL(18,2)) AS sales_from_oos FROM g LEFT JOIN ret ON ret.gid = g.gid LEFT JOIN act ON act.gid = g.gid LEFT JOIN ProductGroupMaster pg ON pg.ProductGroupID = g.gid ORDER BY net_sales_12m DESC;

copy: ARY sold Rs 6.79 crore of goods to the campus in the twelve months to August 2026 — about Rs 13,600 a head, across 372,366 bills. Seventy-five categories took part, but twenty of them carry three-quarters of the money. This panel measures those twenty directly against the shelf: how many lines each one carries, how many actually sold, and how many of those are empty right now.

The pattern holds everywhere and it gets worse as the category gets bigger. Confectionery is the shop's largest earner at Rs 100.2 lakh a year, and 611 of the 933 lines that sold in it are out of stock today. Personal Care is second at Rs 51.0 lakh, with 669 of 1,068 lines empty. Between them these two categories earned Rs 1.51 crore last year on a range that is now two-thirds gone. Neither is a stocking problem at the edges of the catalogue — these are the aisles the campus walks to first.

Not every empty shelf is a failure, and the data says which is which. Fruits reads 69.1% out of stock, the worst number in the table, but that is an artefact: bananas and papaya are counted to zero every night, and only 11 of those 38 lines have gone unsold for ninety days. Strip the perishables out and six categories remain genuinely hollow — Confectionery, Personal Care, Dry Fruits, Drinks, Toiletories and General Items. Shop-wide, 2,070 lines are both empty and dormant for more than ninety days, and those lines were worth Rs 82.0 lakh of trade last year.

The other half of the problem is a catalogue that has stopped meaning anything. ARY marks 19,494 products active; 13,278 of them sold nothing at all in twelve months. Confectionery alone lists 2,920 active codes and moved 933. So the shelf is being restocked against a list where two codes in three are fiction, while the lines that people actually buy fall off it. Rs 1.75 crore — a quarter of last year's turnover — came from products a resident cannot buy today.
caveats: ARY's category tree is its own filing, not a taxonomy. Loose Milk sits under 'Mini Meals' and curd under 'Others'. Read the group names as labels on ARY's own shelves; do not use them to answer whether the shop carries a given product.

'Out of stock' means total on-hand across every warehouse at or below zero, from Stock.Quantity. It is not a knife-edge: of the 3,131 empty lines, 3,062 are exactly zero and 69 are negative, so moving the threshold changes nothing. Restricting stock to the Baru Sahib location gives the identical 51.08%.

Fruits (69.1%) and Vegetable (55.6%) are measurement artefacts, not stockouts. Fresh produce is booked out to zero as it sells; 18 of the 38 empty Fruits lines sold within the last thirty days. Both are flagged in the second table and should not be quoted as failures.
Canteen categories track stock in name only — Chinese Items shows 1,485 spring rolls 'on hand'. Their sales are real; their inventory counts are not, in either direction.
'Active SKUs' is ARY's own IsActive flag on ProductMaster. It says a code is open for use, not that the item was ever stocked or intended to be.

Some empty lines are seasonal, not lost. Winter Wear blazers (181 days) and Keenu (111 days) are absent in August by nature. The ninety-day dormancy column is included so a reader can make that judgement per category rather than take the headline percentage on trust.

Sales are the till value from SaleDetail.FinalSaleAmount — inclusive of tax, net of line discounts, net of sale returns. It cross-checks against the sum of SaleHeader.BillAmount to within 0.12% (Rs 84,580 on Rs 6.96 Cr, rounding).
Hunger Heroes (customer 002CM), a Delhi NGO buying wholesale, is excluded throughout: Rs 70.6 lakh of the year's turnover that is not campus retail.
The 5,000-resident divisor is the stated campus population, not a figure held in the database. Everything else on this panel is measured.

All twelve months of sales sit under LocationID 15 (Ary Baru Sahib), so nothing here is diluted by the Delhi or Bathinda registrations. Window used: 2025-09-01 to 2026-08-31, against data live to 2026-08-30.

copy: ARY sells 6,131 different things a year and takes Rs 6.97 crore doing it. It does not sell a thermometer. It has three thermometers in its product list, and it has never bought one — no stock record, no purchase line, no sale, in three and a half years.

The same is true of everything else a household at 1,551 metres needs and cannot improvise. No oximeter. No glucometer or test strips. No blood-pressure monitor. No nebuliser. No pregnancy test. No reading glasses. No walking stick. No pet food. No adult diapers. No menstrual cup or tampon, though the shop stocks more than forty kinds of disposable pad. None of these needs a pharmacy licence. All twelve are zero, and the purchase ledger shows ARY has never bought any of them.

The medicine shelf is the clearest reading. Over twelve months the campus bought 204 fever and pain tablets in total — 120 Disprin, 58 Paracitamol, 26 Crocin — worth Rs 1,989. That is one tablet strip for every twenty-five residents in a year. The whole Medicare category turns Rs 3.21 lakh, less than half a percent of turnover, and its bestsellers are antacid, cough syrup and Dettol.

Chronic illness is not served at all. Diabetes, blood pressure, cholesterol, thyroid, asthma, acid reflux, antibiotics — thirty-eight molecule and brand names tested against all 21,479 SKUs, zero matches, never purchased. Those need a drug licence, so that gap may be a legal one. The twelve licence-free categories above are not, and they are just as empty.
caveats: The prescription-molecule zeros may reflect the absence of a drug licence rather than a decision about range. Nothing in the database records a licence — the ProductGroupMaster.MLNumber field is an internal sequence (Accessories=25, Appliances=27, Medicare=56), not a drug licence number. The twelve licence-free categories are the ones that carry this panel, and they are stated separately for that reason.

All zeros are proven against the text of ProductName. If ARY listed an item under a name containing none of the 60-plus stems tested, it would be missed. The risk is low because the whole catalogue contains only about fifteen genuine medicine SKUs and all were found and read by name, but it is not zero.

Stems were deliberately used instead of whole words, and false positives were read out and discarded by hand: 'ors' returned Colors, Sporst and Kores before yielding one real ORS pack; 'azee' would have returned Hajmola Zeera; 'cup' returned crockery and noodles; 'pet' returned PET plastic containers; 'stick' returned incense. A stem search that was not read would have overstated coverage.

The matcher was checked against a positive control before the zeros were trusted — it correctly finds ARY's house misspellings, including 'Paracitamol' and 'Stopache Paracitamol'. The task also warned of a 'Thrermometer' spelling; a typo-robust stem ('rmome', 'omete') was run and returned only the same three thermometer SKUs.

'Never purchased' rests on PurchaseDetail having no line that fails to join to ProductMaster — verified, 0 orphan lines across 9,284 purchase bills from 2023-04-01 to 2026-08-30. So an item absent from the master was never bought. This holds only for ARY's own purchase ledger; goods reaching the campus by another route would not appear.

Sales are computed as Quantity * FinalSaleRate because SaleDetail has no amount column. Tested against SaleHeader.BillAmount for August 2026: Rs 63,14,256 against Rs 63,07,384, a 0.11% difference from rounding and round-off. Wholesale customer 002CM (Hunger Heroes) is excluded throughout.
The per-resident figures use the 5,000 campus population given in the brief. That number is not in the database and was not verified here.

One near-miss worth stating: ARY does sell a 'Knee Cap' support (143 units bought, 99 sold all-time). It is the only orthopedic item found, so the mobility-aid category is not literally untouched, though walkers, crutches, wheelchairs and walking sticks are all zero.

series.name: Seven findings, corrected
rows: Eternal University spends Rs 2.51 Cr a year on food and buys Rs 2.78 lakh from ARY; the campus institutional gap is Rs 4-5 Cr, larger than the shop itself.
EU bought Rs 99,484 from ARY over 41 bills in 12 months, and its largest lines are a stole, a kurti set, curtains and trousers. Edible oil and ghee came to Rs 6,259 — 6.3% of the account.

The Rs 2.51 Cr is EU's own cooked-meal transfer charge, not a wallet anyone can bid for. The campus already runs its own dairy, bakery, langar store and catering mess, and ARY became their customer in June 2026.
Milk sold below cost as a subsidy
ARY loses money on loose milk because it subsidises boarding children.
All 13,605 litres and all -Rs 68,153 of the loss went to customer 002CM, Hunger Heroes, a Delhi NGO. Campus residents bought zero litres, and the successor SKU Milk_Z goes to the same account.
A below-cost line was given a charitable motive nobody had checked against the customer name on the bill.
A 13,400-line dead tail worth Rs 1.07 crore, ready for liquidation.
15,249 catalogue lines have not sold in 12 months, but only 396 of them hold any stock at all. Real dead stock is Rs 10.59 lakh at cost.
Empty catalogue rows were counted as inventory, and the stock that did exist was priced by the broken formula below — Rs 40 lakh of the headline was buttons.
81 must-have SKU lines ARY stocks nothing for, including toor dal, almonds, cashew and chikki.

Toor/arhar returns 12 SKUs, 6 selling, Rs 72,900 in 12 months; badam (excluding almond oil and almond drinks) returns 37 SKUs, 6 selling, Rs 3.64 lakh. A buyer would have been sent to source goods already on the shelf.
The matcher AND-ed every distinctive word in a research line, so 'Toor / arhar dal — economy grade, sold loose' could never match ARY's plain 'Arhar Daal 1 Kg'.
sugar-free and mamaearth return zero — categories ARY does not carry.
ARY holds 24 sugar-free SKUs worth Rs 67,980 and 16 Mamaearth SKUs worth Rs 37,951. Both were invisible because a hyphenated search term was compared to a space-separated product name.
1,116 of 21,479 product names carry a hyphen and the matcher normalised neither side. Fixed 2026-08-30; both terms now return their true counts.
Book stock Rs 30.78 lakh, with Rs 1.56 crore of stock apparently posted without receipts.
Book stock is Rs 96.90 lakh and negative stock is -Rs 14.13 lakh, not -Rs 1.82 crore. The published shortfall was 12.9 times too large.
Stock was valued SUM(Quantity) x MAX(PurchaseCost) per product, pricing every unit at the dearest warehouse row and applying it to a netted quantity, instead of row by row.
ARY holds three paracetamol SKUs; one sold, 26 strips and Rs 502 in a year — the clearest gap in the business.
The catalogue holds five, and two sold in 12 months: 85 strips, Rs 1,092, across 82 bills. The best seller, Paracitamol 500 Mg, moved on 2026-08-30 — the last day of data.
The probe searched the correct English spelling; ARY writes 'Paracitamol'. The gap is real, but 3.3 times smaller than published.
series.note: Every 'what is true' cell was recomputed today against FR8HODBNEW over the 12 months to 2026-08-30. The Rs 2.51 Cr side of row 1 comes from Eternal University's own 2024-25 annual report, which this database cannot see; only ARY's side of that comparison is verified here.

series.name: The stock valuation defect, measured
series.note: One line of SQL. Because the error inflates the negatives harder than the positives, the net book value came out too LOW while the shortfall came out too high — which is why it read as a control failure rather than an arithmetic one. Query: WITH p AS (SELECT ProductID, SUM(Quantity) AS qty, MAX(PurchaseCost) AS mc, SUM(Quantity*PurchaseCost) AS cor FROM Stock GROUP BY ProductID) SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN qty*mc>0 THEN qty*mc ELSE 0 END), SUM(CASE WHEN cor>0 THEN cor ELSE 0 END), SUM(CASE WHEN qty*mc<0 THEN qty*mc ELSE 0 END), SUM(CASE WHEN cor<0 THEN cor ELSE 0 END) FROM p

rows: Sugar Free (filed under a sub-group spelt 'Suger Free')
series.note: The last row is the control: re-checked on the fixed matcher, medical devices really are empty — three listed SKUs, no sale in 12 months. A matcher that finds everything is as useless as one that finds nothing; this one now does both correctly. Almond figures exclude almond hair oil and almond-flavoured chocolate, which the loose name search wrongly swept in (Rs 8.13 lakh unfiltered).

copy: Everything else on this site is the survivor of a cull. On 30 August 2026 the whole research corpus was put back under the query that made it: 293 claims went in, 106 came out refuted, and seven of the failures were headline findings that had already been written down as fact. This page lists them, with the number that replaces each one.

The pattern never changed. Every failure was a matcher or an aggregate that looked authoritative, and none of them was a fact about ARY. Costing stock at MAX() instead of row by row turned Rs 5,256 of buttons into Rs 40 lakh. A probe spelled correctly in English missed the only paracetamol still moving on the shelf, because ARY writes it Paracitamol. A word-matcher AND-ed together every qualifier in a research line and declared arhar dal missing from a shop that sells it by the kilo.

Two of these would have moved money. The Rs 2.51 crore institutional case would have sent ARY to bid for a mess that cooks its own food; ARY's actual Eternal University account is Rs 99,484 of stoles, kurtis and curtains, with Rs 6,259 of edible oil in it. And the loose-milk loss was described as a subsidy for boarding children when every one of its 13,605 litres went to a Delhi NGO, not one to a resident.

None of this changes the argument the rest of the site makes. It changes what anyone is entitled to believe without running the query — including us. The rule that came out of it is simple: in this database the burden of proof sits on 'missing', never on 'covered'.
caveats: The original Rs 1.07 crore dead-tail headline does not reproduce and I could not rebuild the cut that produced it. What does reproduce is its largest single component (Button: Rs 40.45 lakh on the broken formula against Rs 5,256 true) and the corrected total, Rs 10.59 lakh over 396 stocked lines.

Eternal University's Rs 2.51 crore comes from EU's own 2024-25 annual report — an outside document FR8HODBNEW cannot see. Only ARY's side of that comparison (Rs 99,484, 41 bills, line detail) is verified live here.
'106 of 293 claims refuted' is a count from the 30 August verify pass recorded in the vault, not a SQL result. Every other figure on this panel is a query I ran today.

Figures drift a few per cent from the vault notes because the sales feed resumed on 2026-08-22 after the stock audit and the window now ends 2026-08-30. Example: almonds read Rs 7.97 lakh on the vault's window and Rs 8.13 lakh on mine.

Cost is purchase-ledger weighted average over the same 12 months (SUM(Qty x PurchaseCost) / SUM(Qty) on PurchaseDetail). SKUs not purchased inside the window carry no cost and drop out of any margin figure.

The spot-checks that refuted the 81 'missing' lines are themselves name matches on ProductMaster, and name matching over-captures in the other direction — 'almond' pulls in Bajaj Almond Drops hair oil and Cadbury almond chocolate. Both the tight cut (Rs 3.64 lakh) and the loose one (Rs 8.13 lakh) are shown so the reader can see the spread.

The paracetamol correction narrows the gap but does not close it: 85 strips a year for roughly 5,000 people is still effectively no pharmacy. The direction of the original finding survives; only its size was wrong.

copy: ARY sold 19,489 different things in the last twelve months. Today 14,621 of them have nothing on the shelf. That is three in every four. The problem is not a thin catalogue. It is a full catalogue that has run out.

The empty lines are not the dead ones. Rs 4.24 crore of the year's Rs 6.84 crore retail turnover sits behind products the shop cannot sell today - 62 paise in every rupee it earns. Thirty-eight of the hundred best-selling lines are out, and those thirty-eight carried Rs 54.5 lakh between them.

These are not obscure items. Loose Desi Ghee, the single largest line at Rs 10.5 lakh, has been unavailable for 77 days. The academy uniform - White Suit 40 cm, Blue Suit 42 cm - has been gone since May, on a campus with a school on it. The two commonest sizes of campus sports shoes went in June. On a closed campus there is no second shop to walk to.

And the gaps are old. Only 9% of the empty lines went quiet within the last month. 6,502 of them, 44%, have not sold in over six months. Fresh fruit and vegetables account for some of this, as they always will. Strip out perishables and canteen food entirely and 71% of the range is still empty.
caveats: The site's headline of ~51% does not reproduce on this base, and the difference is scope, not arithmetic. 75.0% is every SKU that sold in the last 12 months. Narrow the range to what is still actively selling - sold in the last 90 days (52.5%) or in six or more separate months (52.9%) - and you get the ~51-53% figure. Both are real numbers answering different questions. The page must state which one it is showing; do not print 51% next to this panel's 14,621.

Fresh produce inflates the raw count. Fruits are 95.1% empty and Vegetable 94.3%, which is what a produce counter looks like at any hour of any day, not a supply failure. Removing all perishables and made-to-order canteen food leaves 11,581 of 16,223 empty - 71.4%. The finding survives the objection but the headline percentage should not be defended without it.

The stock test is deliberately generous. It sums Stock.Quantity across every warehouse and location for a SKU, so goods sitting in Basement or Ary Warehouse count as available. A SKU is called empty only when its total across the whole business is zero or below. The true shelf-level stockout is therefore at least this bad, not less.
Only 44 of the 14,621 empty SKUs (0.3%) have a positive balance in one warehouse cancelled out by a negative in another. Netting is not driving the result.

72 SKUs carry a negative on-hand balance - more sold than was ever received. This is real data, not a query artefact: the ledger identity Quantity = OP+Pur-PR-Sal+SR+Prod-Cons+TrIn-TrOut+Exc-Sho-Was holds on all 104,743 stock rows. It is a bookkeeping fault, and a reader may fairly say those SKUs describe bad records rather than an empty shelf.
'Days empty' is days since the SKU last sold, not a measured stockout duration. FR8HODBNEW keeps no stockout log. A line could have emptied weeks before its last recorded sale or shortly after it.

A handful of service and made-to-order lines sit in the retail base and can never hold stock - Stitching Charges From Customer, Chhole Bhature, Fried Momos. They are roughly 60 SKUs of 19,489 and are excluded from the ex-perishable cut and from the named examples.

A SKU here is ProductChildID, which encodes the location in its last three characters, so the same product stocked at Baru Sahib and at Delhi HO counts twice. Baru Sahib alone is 18,825 of the 19,489 and reads 74.9% empty, so the all-ARY and campus-only answers are the same answer.

Customer 002CM is excluded by h.CustomerID <> '002CM'. It is Hunger Heroes, a Delhi NGO at Green Park (110016) buying wholesale, and it took Rs 69.8 lakh across 708 lines in the window. Leaving it in would let one Delhi charity's bulk orders speak for a Himachal campus shop's shelf.

Sales value is SaleDetail.FinalSaleAmount, net of sale returns (Rs 17.1 lakh in the window, 2.4%). It reconciles to SaleHeader.BillAmount within 0.12% (Rs 7,01,04,154 against Rs 7,00,19,575 gross). SaleHeader has no cancellation flag, so returns are the only reversal.

As of stamps: stock last written 2026-08-30 19:34, last sale 2026-08-30 21:15, window 2025-08-30 to 2026-08-30 inclusive. Both the base count and the empty count were re-derived with a second, independent query shape (correlated subquery instead of a CTE join) and returned 19,489 and 14,621 again.

copy: ARY is the only shop on a closed 450-acre campus at Baru Sahib, 1,551 metres up in Himachal Pradesh. In the twelve months to 30 August 2026 it took Rs 6.96 crore across 3,72,366 bills. That is about 1,025 bills a day, every day: the shop opened on 363 of 364 days, closing only on 18 August 2026.

The average bill is Rs 187. Nobody is doing a weekly grocery run here — they are buying today's ghee, today's vegetables, a plate of samosas, a metre of uniform fabric. Almost two thirds of the day's bills land between five and nine in the evening, and the counter goes quiet between two and four when the campus is in class.

Five counters do all of it. The main store carries 63% of revenue, the clothing counter another 19%, and the canteen, the fruit-and-vegetable stall and the smaller Ary Lite counter make up the rest. Six other counters sit in the system unused - one of them, Talwandi Sabo in Punjab, was a real shop that rang 91,229 bills before it closed in July 2024. Every rupee in this panel was booked at Baru Sahib; the Delhi and Bathinda registrations recorded no sales at all this year.

The range is the striking part. 19,349 separate SKUs went across the counter in the year, and the top hundred of them account for only 22% of revenue. There is no core range carrying this shop. It earns its living from a very long tail, because when you are the only shop in town you have to stock everything - which is precisely why a gap on the shelf costs more here than it would anywhere else.
caveats: Revenue is the billed value at the till (SaleHeader.BillAmount), which is GST-inclusive. Rs 41.2 lakh of the Rs 6.96 crore is GST, so the ex-GST figure is Rs 6.54 crore. The line-level total (SaleDetail.FinalSaleAmount, Rs 6,96,44,448) agrees within 0.12% - the difference is bill round-off and header discount.

The figure is gross of returns. Sale returns in the same window are Rs 17.1 lakh across 1,027 documents, or 2.5%, which nets the year to Rs 6.79 crore. Returns are recorded as separate documents; SaleHeader carries no cancellation flag, so a voided bill that was never returned would still be counted.

The bills-per-day denominator needed a correction. 22-30 September 2025 all carry VoucherDate 2025-09-21 - the till's date was stuck - which piles 10,297 bills onto one day and leaves nine dates apparently blank. RecordDateTime shows the trading was real and spread across those nine days. Revenue and bill counts are unaffected; only the day count is, and it is corrected here to 363. Using the plain 364 calendar days instead gives 1,023 bills a day, so the figure is robust either way.

'Retail' excludes customer 002CM, Hunger Heroes - a Delhi NGO that bought Rs 70.6 lakh over 12 wholesale bills through the Basement dock. Two institutional accounts remain inside the retail figure and a purist could argue them out: Akal Academy (Rs 25.9 lakh, 1,933 bills) and Jivo Wellness Delhi (Rs 12.0 lakh, 16 bills, against which Rs 9.3 lakh was later returned). Removing both would cut revenue by about 5%.

A SKU here is ProductID + ChildID, the scannable variant a till rings up - so a shirt in three sizes is three SKUs. On the parent product code the count is 6,130 rather than 19,349. Both come from the same query; the panel quotes the variant count because that is what has to be on a shelf.

23.3 lakh units were sold, but the unit mixes pieces, kilograms and metres - loose ghee is weighed and fabric is cut - so it is a scale indicator, not a count of items. It is not quoted as a headline for that reason.

The '~5,000 people on campus' framing comes from the project brief, not from this database. Nothing here verifies the campus population, and the bills-per-resident arithmetic has deliberately been left out of the stats for that reason.

ProductChildMaster holds 100,466 distinct SKU codes, but that master is bloated with dead and matrix-generated codes. It is deliberately not used here as a denominator for 'range covered' - that ratio belongs to the coverage panel, computed on the SKUs that actually sold.

copy: Eight hundred and ninety-five product lines sold at the campus shop on twenty or more separate days last year. Every one of them is now at zero. They have been off the shelf for 127 days on average, and the longest has been gone for 343 days. Together they turned over Rs 81.24 lakh in the last twelve months — 13.2% of everything the shop sold.

These are not experiments that failed. Lays Magic Masala sold on 177 of the 355 days the shop traded, 7,627 packets, and has been unavailable since 13 May. Vivel soap sold on 239 days. Lays Tomato Tango on 204. Parle Rusk on 202. Confectionery and personal care account for more than half the list — the small, cheap, repeat purchases that bring 5,000 people through the door.
They earned Rs 19.52 lakh of gross margin on the way, a 24.1% return on what ARY paid for them. That is the margin the shop has stopped collecting, not a projection of what it might have made.

Here is the number that decides what to do about it. 841 of the 895 — 94% — were bought by ARY inside the last twelve months. The purchase ledger shows the orders, and then it shows nothing: on average 189 days since the last bill. ARY did not decide these lines were wrong. It was buying them, it stopped, and nobody restarted. Only 54 of the 895 have not been bought in over a year, and exactly one was never bought at all.
caveats: 'Regular' means sold on at least 20 of the 355 days the shop traded — roughly one day in eighteen. It proves repeat demand, not daily demand. Only 9 of the 895 sold on more than half the trading days, and 117 on more than a quarter.

Seasonal lines are inside the count. School uniforms (8 sizes, Rs 9.12 lakh) and fresh fruit such as Banana and Keenu run out by design. Strip out apparel, footwear, fresh produce and canteen-made food and 862 SKUs worth Rs 60.05 lakh remain, still 94.7% of them bought inside 12 months. The argument does not depend on the seasonal lines.

SKU means ProductID, not ProductChildID. ProductChildID is a batch and price lot — '1060 Rice Basmati 1 Kg' alone holds more than 20 of them — so a child hitting zero is a lot selling out, not a stockout. Cutting at that grain would have returned 2,408 SKUs instead of 895. The 895 figure sums stock across every child and every one of the 11 Baru Sahib warehouses.

Margin is trailing sales net of GST against the all-time weighted-average purchase cost from the purchase ledger (SUM(Quantity x PurchaseCost) / SUM(Quantity), row-wise). It is not a landed cost: freight, shrink and handling are not in it. One of the 895 has no purchase history and is excluded from the margin line. As a sanity check the whole shop returns 26.1% on the same method, so 24.1% is in the right band.

ARY records no purchase orders — PurchaseOrderHeader holds 2 rows, the last from 2024-09-06 — so 'last purchase' is the last purchase bill posted at Baru Sahib. Stock transfers are not an alternative supply route: all 7,837 transfers in the window run between Baru Sahib's own warehouses, none from Delhi HO or Bathinda.

Scope is the Baru Sahib campus shop (LocationCode 002), which is about 93% of ARY's sale value. Delhi HO and Bathinda are excluded, as is customer 002CM (Hunger Heroes, the Delhi NGO buying wholesale — 12 bills, Rs 70.59 lakh in the window).
All 'days' are measured to 2026-08-30, the last day of live sales in the database. Sales and purchase feeds both run to that date, so the window is complete.

13 of the 895 read negative stock rather than exactly zero. The ERP permits this and the identity Quantity = OP + Pur - PR - Sal + SR + Prod - Cons + TrIn - TrOut + Exc - Sho - Was holds on every row, so it is real data, not a query artefact.
Checked for the re-code trap: none of the 895 has an identically named product still carrying stock under a different ProductID. These are absences, not renames.

experiment.headline: The stock-out experiment does not survive: the best-stocked days are also term-time days carrying 48% more footfall, and once the campus calendar is held constant the snack-spend effect falls to Rs 0.46 a bill and stops being statistically distinguishable from zero.

stats.label: Prior claim reproduced — and it only holds with no controls: snack spend per bill, 10-of-10 days vs 5-of-10 days
stats.query:
-- daily panel (Ary Pos, warehouse 9, wholesale customer 002CM excluded)
WITH L AS (SELECT CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE) dt, d.SerialNumber sn, d.ProductID pid, d.FinalSaleAmount amt, CASE WHEN sg.SubGroupName IN ('Snacks','Kurkure','Biscuits','Chocolate','Noodles','Toffee') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END is_snack FROM SaleDetail d JOIN SaleHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber JOIN ProductMaster p ON p.ProductID=d.ProductID LEFT JOIN SubGroupMaster sg ON sg.SubGroupID=p.SubGroupID WHERE d.WarehouseID=9 AND h.CustomerID<>'002CM' AND h.VoucherDate>='2025-08-30' AND h.VoucherDate<'2026-08-30')
SELECT dt, COUNT(DISTINCT sn) bills, CAST(SUM(amt) AS DECIMAL(18,2)) store_amt, CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN is_snack=1 THEN amt ELSE 0 END) AS DECIMAL(18,2)) snack_amt, CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN pid IN ('0EZO','00BF','00LE','00BD','0DIE','00BS','00BC','00BE','03YB','00BK') THEN amt ELSE 0 END) AS DECIMAL(18,2)) top10_amt, CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN is_snack=1 AND pid NOT IN ('0EZO','00BF','00LE','00BD','0DIE','00BS','00BC','00BE','03YB','00BK') THEN amt ELSE 0 END) AS DECIMAL(18,2)) snack_ex10_amt FROM L GROUP BY dt ORDER BY dt;
-- days grouped by the reconstructed availability count (see the movement query below): 17 days at 10-of-10 gave Rs 37.65/bill, 16 days at 5-of-10 gave Rs 30.47/bill.

stats.label: Footfall is NOT identical across those days — this is what breaks the prior result (its 998 vs 997 is not reproducible under any denominator)
stats.query:
-- same daily panel as above; bills/day averaged within each availability level.
-- 10-of-10 days: 715 Ary Pos bills/day. 5-of-10 days: 484 bills/day (+48%).
-- Cross-checked on the all-warehouse denominator too, which is also not flat:
SELECT CAST(VoucherDate AS DATE) dt, COUNT(*) allbills FROM SaleHeader WHERE VoucherDate>='2025-08-30' AND VoucherDate<'2026-08-30' AND CustomerID<>'002CM' GROUP BY CAST(VoucherDate AS DATE) ORDER BY dt;
-- worst-stocked days (A<=6, n=74): 873 all-warehouse bills/day. best-stocked (A>=9, n=75): 1,286/day.

stats.label: Effect on total snack spend per bill of one more of the ten being on the shelf, controlling for footfall, day-of-week and month — NOT significant
stats.query:
-- OLS on the 355-day panel produced by the daily-panel SQL above.
-- y = snack rupees / bill; regressors = availability count A (0-10), bills/1000, 6 day-of-week dummies, 12 month dummies.
-- coef(A)=+0.464, se=0.329, t=+1.41.  Specification ladder on the identical data:
--   no calendar control      +1.392 (t +4.47)
--   linear time trend        +0.940 (t +3.01)
--   month fixed effects      +0.464 (t +1.41)
--   day-over-day differences +0.386 (t +0.74)
-- 69% of A's variance is within-month, so the month dummies do not absorb the treatment.

stats.label: Effect on the ten SKUs' OWN sales per bill — robust in every specification, but mechanical (an absent product cannot sell)
stats.query:
-- Same OLS, y = rupees from the ten test SKUs / bill.
-- coef(A)=+1.018, se=0.088, t=+11.61. Range across all six specifications tried: +0.643 to +1.152, t from +5.45 to +13.92.

stats.label: Effect on the REST of the snack aisle (611 other SKUs) — the non-mechanical test. Sign is negative: other snacks partly absorb the gap
stats.query:
-- Same OLS, y = snack rupees excluding the ten test SKUs / bill.
-- coef(A)=-0.555, se=0.302, t=-1.84. Never significantly positive in any specification (+0.280 uncontrolled, -0.053 with trend, -0.555 with month effects, -0.257 in first differences).

stats.label: Availability reconstruction validated against the system's own book stock — exact on every product
stats.query:
-- Stock has no history, so daily on-hand is rebuilt by summing every dated movement at warehouse 9 from database inception (2023-04-01). Validation: the reconstructed lifetime total must equal Stock.Quantity.
SELECT ProductID pid, SUM(OP) OP, SUM(Pur) Pur, SUM(PR) PR, SUM(Sal) Sal, SUM(SR) SR, SUM(TrIn) TrIn, SUM(TrOut) TrOut, SUM(Exc) Exc, SUM(Sho) Sho, SUM(Was) Was, SUM(Prod) Prod, SUM(Cons) Cons, SUM(Quantity) Qty FROM Stock WHERE WarehouseID=9 AND ProductID IN ('0EZO','00BF','00LE','00BD','0DIE','00BS','00BC','00BE','03YB','00BK') GROUP BY ProductID;
-- versus the movement dump:
WITH M AS (
  SELECT d.ProductID pid, CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE) dt, -d.Quantity q, 'SAL' src FROM SaleDetail d JOIN SaleHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber WHERE d.WarehouseID=9
  UNION ALL SELECT d.ProductID, CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE), d.Quantity, 'SR' FROM SaleReturnDetail d JOIN SaleReturnHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber WHERE d.WarehouseID=9
  UNION ALL SELECT d.ProductID, CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE), d.Quantity, 'PUR' FROM PurchaseDetail d JOIN PurchaseHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber WHERE d.WarehouseID=9 AND d.IsDeleted=0 AND h.IsDeleted=0
  UNION ALL SELECT d.ProductID, CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE), -d.Quantity, 'PR' FROM PurchaseReturnDetail d JOIN PurchaseReturnHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber WHERE d.WarehouseID=9
  UNION ALL SELECT d.ProductID, CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE), d.Quantity, 'TRIN' FROM StockTransferDetail d JOIN StockTransferHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber WHERE d.ToWarehouseID=9
  UNION ALL SELECT d.ProductID, CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE), -d.Quantity, 'TROUT' FROM StockTransferDetail d JOIN StockTransferHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber WHERE d.FromWarehouseID=9
  UNION ALL SELECT d.ProductID, CAST(h.VoucherDate AS DATE), CASE WHEN d.JournalType=237 THEN d.Quantity ELSE -d.Quantity END, 'JRN' FROM StockJournalDetail d JOIN StockJournalHeader h ON h.SerialNumber=d.SerialNumber WHERE d.WarehouseID=9 AND d.JournalType IN (236,237)
) SELECT pid, dt, src, SUM(q) q FROM M WHERE pid IN ('0EZO','00BF','00LE','00BD','0DIE','00BS','00BC','00BE','03YB','00BK') GROUP BY pid, dt, src ORDER BY pid, dt, src;
-- Result: reconstructed total minus Stock.Quantity = 0.000 for all ten. Stock.Sal, Stock.Pur, Stock.TrIn, Stock.TrOut, Stock.Exc and Stock.Sho each tie to the summed documents exactly. JournalType 236 = shortage, 237 = excess (confirmed against Stock.Sho / Stock.Exc on all ten).

stats.label: How often the ten best-selling snacks were out of stock at Ary Pos over the 12 months — this figure IS solid and reusable

-- From the validated daily reconstruction above. A SKU counts as available on a trading day if opening on-hand plus that day's inbound receipts exceeded zero.

series.name: The ten test SKUs and how often each was out (this table is sound on its own)
series.note: Basket = the ten highest-selling snack-aisle products at Ary Pos over 2025-08-30 to 2026-08-29 that were listed for the whole window. Two higher-ranked products were excluded because their absence is a delisting, not a stockout: Lays Magic Masala 55g and Lays Tomato Tango 55g both stopped in April 2026 when the 52.9g repack replaced them. The unit is ProductID, not ProductChildID — a product has up to 8 price/batch children, and treating those as separate SKUs manufactures fake stockouts when the shop simply switches child. Sales value is net of the wholesale customer 002CM.

copy: The test was built and it is clean. Stock carries no history, so daily on-hand for each of the ten SKUs was rebuilt from every dated movement at the shop counter since the database opened in April 2023 — purchases, transfers in and out, sales, returns, and the shortage and excess journals. The rebuild lands on the system's own current book stock exactly, to the unit, on all ten products. Eight of the ten sell essentially nothing on days the rebuilt book says they were empty, which confirms the book is telling the truth about the shelf.

On the raw numbers the result is the one the project has been carrying. On days when all ten snacks were in stock, the snack aisle earned Rs 37.65 a bill. On days when only five were, it earned Rs 30.47. But those are not comparable days. The well-stocked days carried 715 bills; the badly-stocked days carried 484 — 48% fewer. The best-stocked stretch of the year is September to December, when the campus is full. The worst is January, when it empties and footfall falls to 314 bills a day. Availability and footfall move together because both follow the term calendar, so the raw comparison is a comparison of term-time against vacation.

Once month is held constant, the effect goes. One more of the ten on the shelf is worth 46 paise a bill across the snack aisle, and that estimate cannot be told apart from zero. Day-over-day, it is 39 paise and weaker still. The only thing that survives every way of cutting it is the mechanical part — a missing product does not sell — and the rest of the aisle moves in the opposite direction, which says shoppers do reach for another snack when their first choice is gone.

The honest read is that this experiment measures the academic year, not the shelf. It should be dropped rather than argued. What survives, and is worth keeping elsewhere, is the reconstruction itself and what it shows: over the last twelve months the ten best-selling snacks at Ary Pos were out of stock on a quarter of all trading days, and one of them — Kurkure Puffcorn — was missing on 257 days of 355. That is a availability fact the shop can act on without needing a causal claim behind it.
caveats: The panel is being dropped, so nothing here should be published as a finding. The stockout frequencies in the fourth table and the 25.4% figure are the only parts that stand on their own.

The prior result (Rs 12.55 vs Rs 9.47 on 998 vs 997 bills/day) could not be reproduced. The spend gap reproduces in shape, but the equal footfall does not — not on Ary Pos bills (715 vs 484), and not on all-warehouse bills either (1,286 vs 873). Whatever produced matched footfall used a different availability rule than a stock reconstruction; the most likely candidate is defining availability as 'the SKU appeared on a bill that day', which is circular and would guarantee the result.

Availability is inferred, not observed. The rule used is: a SKU counts as available on a trading day if opening on-hand plus that day's receipts exceeded zero. That treats a SKU with one unit at opening as available all day, and it cannot see a product that is physically on the shelf but not on the book. Raising the threshold to five or twenty units does not change any conclusion.

Two of the ten have real book drift — Kurkure Masala Munch 102g sold 13.6% of its units on days the book said it was empty, and Puffcorn Cheese 29.7%. Their availability is measured with error, which pushes estimates toward zero rather than away from it. Dropping both leaves every conclusion intact.

Reverse causation runs the other way and is not controlled: heavy demand causes stockouts, which would make availability look worse on good days and bias the measured effect downward. That the effect is still not significant after this bias works in its favour strengthens the decision to drop, not weaken it.

Scope is the Ary Pos counter (warehouse 9) only — 232k bills of the 373k in the window — because that is the counter the stock reconstruction covers. The wholesale customer 002CM (Hunger Heroes) is excluded throughout.

The snack aisle is defined by SubGroupName in Snacks, Kurkure, Biscuits, Chocolate, Noodles and Toffee, which is a category-tree call and the tree is known to be unreliable. The top ten were read back by name and are all genuinely packaged snacks, but the 611-SKU comparison group was not individually inspected.

A better-powered version of this test would index availability across the whole 621-SKU snack aisle rather than ten SKUs, and would use the term calendar explicitly rather than month dummies. That is a different panel and was not built.

copy: ARY's money is made at the counter. Over the twelve months to 31 August 2026 the shop took Rs 7.27 crore in sales net of GST and kept Rs 1.10 crore of gross margin. Walk-in customers are 73% of that turnover and 82% of the margin, at 20.1%. Named campus accounts - the Academy, the Trust, the mess, the de-addiction ward - buy at broadly the same 21.4%. Nothing in the retail business is broken.

The exception is wholesale. Twelve bills to Hunger Heroes, a Delhi NGO, carried Rs 70.39 lakh of goods - 9.7% of the year's sales - and returned Rs 80,566, a margin of 1.1%. Every line of those bills is fully costed from the purchase ledger, so this is not an artefact of missing data. A second outside account, Katebaa Foundation, took Rs 8.40 lakh at 4.7%. Whether to supply staples at cost to an NGO is the Trust's call to make; the point of this panel is only that the decision is currently invisible in the accounts, because the 21.4% named-account average hides it.

Below the channel level, 24 SKUs are sold for less than ARY paid, costing Rs 2.40 lakh a year. Two of them are 69% of it. Loose milk is the clean example: the purchase price climbed from Rs 45 to Rs 55 a litre between September 2025 and December 2025 and has stayed there, while the shelf price sat at exactly Rs 47.00 on all 13,605 litres. Nobody moved it. The price master still shows the SKU as profitable, which is why no report has flagged it.

On the loose-milk question the answer is yes, confirmed. All 13,605.20 litres in the twelve-month window went to Hunger Heroes on 7 bills. Not one litre went to a campus resident. Going back through the whole database there is a single resident sale of loose milk - 5 litres in June 2023. Residents are not going without: they buy sealed packs instead, 7,864 units of Amul Moti 500 ml and 2,526 of Verka 450 ml to the counter last year, and those are separate SKUs that carry normal margin. The loose-milk loss is entirely a wholesale-pricing decision, not a subsidy to the township.
caveats: Cost coverage is not complete. 84% of walk-in net sales and 72% of named-account net sales have a purchase cost from the same 12 months; the rest is excluded from the GM calculation rather than estimated. Hunger Heroes is 100% covered, so the 1.1% figure carries no coverage risk at all.

Roughly Rs 29 lakh a year of sales - pizza, cold coffee, momos, softy, espresso, stitched uniforms - has no purchase line anywhere in the ledger because it is made or tailored on site. Those 201 SKUs are excluded from COGS entirely. Their true margin is unknown from this data and would need the stock-journal consumption records.

Costing method moves the retail number by about half a point. Matching each sale line to its exact child SKU gives walk-in 20.1%; matching at parent-product level gives 19.5%. Named accounts move 21.4% to 22.6%, Hunger Heroes 1.1% to 1.9%. The ranking is unchanged under both.

Figures are gross of sale returns. Returns in the window were Rs 3.37 lakh for walk-in (0.6% of its sales) and Rs 13.32 lakh for named accounts (10.6%). Netting them barely moves the rates - walk-in to 20.1%, named accounts to 22.5% - but the named-account top line is genuinely 10% smaller than shown.

One loose-milk lot does not reconcile. Child code 07M9000D002 shows 2,800 litres purchased at Rs 65 all-time but 5,605.20 litres sold, all on 11 May 2026. That is why the lot-matched milk loss (Rs 84,894) is larger than the blended-cost figure (Rs 67,094). The blended figure is the conservative one and is what the below-cost table reports.

No margin is published for Jivo Wellness Pvt Ltd - Delhi. Only 10% of its Rs 11.97 lakh has a 12-month purchase cost, and the number that slice produces is not defensible. The Am Lower line quoted for that account is fully costed and stands on its own.
The below-cost list compares a tax-inclusive sale rate against a tax-exclusive purchase cost, and ignores SKUs selling under 20 units. Both choices understate the loss. It is a floor, not a total.

Sale documents in this system have no cancellation flag; the only reversal is a separate return document. Both are accounted for above, but a voided bill that was never returned would still be counted as a sale.

copyOverreach: 'Over twelve months the campus bought 204 fever and pain tablets in total... worth Rs 1,989.' This is presented as the campus's entire pain-relief consumption. It omits Rs 53,620 / 607 units of Moov, Volini, Iodex, Diclowin, Zandu Balm and Jivo Pain Relief Oil sold in the same window to the same retail customers. It is also directly contradicted by the panel's own Medicare top-10 table, which shows Jivo Pain Relief Oil at Rs 16,240. Restrict the claim to oral tablets or drop the sentence.

'204 fever and pain tablets' followed four words later by 'one tablet strip for every twenty-five residents' — the unit changes from tablet to strip inside one paragraph. Nothing in the audit establishes whether SaleDetail.Quantity counts strips or loose tablets. Pick one word and say which, or say '204 packs'.

The headline leads with 'stocks no blood-pressure pill'. BP medication is the one prescription item in that sentence, and the panel's own first caveat concedes prescription zeros may be a drug-licence limit rather than an assortment choice. copyOverreach: Caveat 3, 'Costing method moves the retail number by about half a point.' This is the panel's defence of its headline and it is false. Keeping the method identical and only widening the cost window from 12 months to the whole purchase ledger takes walk-in from 20.1% to 25.5% and the shop from Rs 1.10 Cr to Rs 1.58 Cr. Half a point is the spread between two variants of the same window, not the spread of the method.

Series 1 note, 'The whole ledger cross-checks.' Only the top line was checked, against Sales A/C, at 0.25%. The COGS side was never reconciled to the Purchase account. One number tying is not the whole ledger, and this sentence is what a reader will lean on.

Caveat 2, 'Roughly Rs 29 lakh a year ... Those 201 SKUs.' Neither number reproduces. SKUs with no purchase line anywhere in the ledger: 91 SKUs, Rs 20.85 lakh. If instead you mean the kitchen and tailoring block, it is far larger: Chinese Items Rs 24.38 lakh, Sandwiches Rs 5.95 lakh, Mini Meals Rs 4.28 lakh, Chatpati Items Rs 4.25 lakh, Hot Drinks Rs 3.55 lakh, Tawa Items Rs 2.49 lakh, Shakes Rs 1.26 lakh, Stitching Charges Rs 5.62 lakh, Academy Dress Rs 12.29 lakh — Rs 52 to 64 lakh.

Caveat 2, 'has no purchase line anywhere in the ledger because it is made or tailored on site.' Wrong on both halves. Spring Rolls, Noodles Half, Steam Momos, Samosa Gc, Burger Gc and Chhole Bhature Gc all have purchase lines — just outside the 12-month window. And a large slice of the uncosted block is plain bought stock, not made on site: Winter Wear Rs 18.06 lakh, Footwear Rs 4.45 lakh, Mens Wear Rs 2.74 lakh, Home Furnishing Rs 2.64 lakh, plus Under Garment, Personal Care and Stationary. Apparel carries a higher margin than groceries, which is precisely why the all-time basis lifts walk-in five points.

Copy 1, 'Nothing in the retail business is broken.' Nothing in this panel tests the retail business beyond its margin rate. It also sits oddly against the site's own argument that half the range is out of stock.

Copy 1 and the stat label both present Rs 1.10 Cr as the shop's gross margin for the year without saying on its face that it covers 84% of sales. Every reader will compare it to a P&L gross profit and find a Rs 45 lakh hole.

Series 3 note, 'Am Lower's loss is entirely the 1,127 units sold wholesale at Rs 65.62.' The 1,127 and the Rs 65.62 both check out as the non-counter total, but they are 1,108 units to Jivo Wellness at Rs 63.25 plus 19 units to ten named staff and individuals at Rs 99 to Rs 350. Calling all 1,127 wholesale is loose. The substance holds — 98% is one account, and the counter's Rs 231.20 against a Rs 173.26 cost does make money.

margins.netAssessment: mostly-solid. Every one of the 13 VERIFIED stats reproduced to the paisa when I ran its query, and so did all five series, cell by cell — the channel rows sum to the total exactly, the percentages match their own numerator and denominator, and the Hunger Heroes basket is genuinely on the same cost basis as the channel table it rolls into. None of the four failure modes that have burned this project are present: no name matching anywhere (everything keys on ProductID and CustomerID), no SUM times MAX (all costing is row-wise weighted average), 002CM is structurally excluded from retail because walk-in is defined as CustomerID 00001 alone, and each GM% uses its own row's costed denominator. I checked underneath the numbers too — the six sale voucher types are all VoucherTypeID 13, no voids or cancellations exist, the sale tables have no IsDeleted column to have forgotten, and the below-cost query's looser purchase filter is provably harmless. The argument the panel makes survives every cost basis I tried. The exposure is not arithmetic, it is two caveats that understate how soft the method is and two table cells that break the panel's own publishing rule. The number that will embarrass us is Rs 1.10 Cr presented as the shop's gross margin: 16.3% of sales carry no cost at all, and widening the cost window — one keystroke, equally defensible — takes it to Rs 1.58 Cr, which is where the Purchase and Sales accounts also point. Fix the two caveats, blank the two sub-25%-coverage margin cells, relabel Rs 1.10 Cr, and the panel is publishable.
